common_name: Carver Sweet Potato (George Washington Carver Heirloom)

planting.note: Set rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost into ridged, loose soil in full sun; Carver is a mid-20th-century Southern release named in honor of George Washington Carver, grown for dependable yields of deep orange, blocky roots.

directions: Set slips into ridged, well-drained soil two to four weeks after the last frost, spacing plants a foot to eighteen inches apart along the row. Carver was developed and released in the mid-1900s as a disease-tolerant Southern market type with deep rose-copper skin and deep orange, moderately moist flesh, and carries the name of George Washington Carver in recognition of his sweet potato research and promotion work at Tuskegee Institute. Vines are vigorous and roots size up fairly uniformly, making the variety a steady producer for home gardeners who want a classic baking sweet potato without heavy disease pressure. Dig before the first hard frost, cure for a week to ten days at warm, humid conditions, and store cool and dry to sweeten the flesh.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America
USDA National Agricultural Library — George Washington Carver Historical Publications

common_name: Jersey Orange Sweet Potato (Orange-Fleshed Jersey Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in loose, ridged soil; Jersey Orange is the orange-fleshed counterpart to the drier-fleshed White and Yellow Jersey sweet potato types once common along the Mid-Atlantic coast.

directions: Plant rooted slips into raised, loosened ridges two to four weeks after the last frost date, in full sun. Jersey Orange belongs to the old Jersey group of sweet potatoes grown historically along the New Jersey and Delmarva coastal plain, sharing the group's orange-brown skin but distinguished from its White Jersey and Yellow Jersey relatives by deep orange, sweeter flesh instead of the drier, starchier texture typical of Jersey types. The vines are moderately vigorous and the roots tend toward a tapered, uniform shape that stores well. Harvest before frost damages the vines, cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for about a week, then move to cool, dry storage.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost into loose, ridged soil; Darby is a Louisiana-bred release selected for resistance to fusarium wilt and soil rot, with dark rose skin and orange flesh.

directions: Set slips into ridged, well-worked soil two to four weeks after the last frost, spacing a foot to eighteen inches apart. Darby is a Louisiana sweet potato breeding program release carrying dark rose skin over orange flesh on blocky-shaped roots held on vines with purple stems, selected in part for resistance to fusarium wilt and soil rot that can otherwise shorten a planting's productive life in warm, humid soils. The resistance package makes it a useful choice for gardeners replanting sweet potatoes in the same bed in consecutive seasons. Dig before frost touches the vines, cure for about a week in warm, humid conditions to heal the skin, then store cool and dry.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

common_name: Travis Sweet Potato (Early White-Fleshed Market Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost; Travis is an early-maturing white-fleshed sweet potato released for local fresh-market and garden use through North Carolina Foundation Seed Producers.

directions: Plant slips into loose, ridged soil two to four weeks after the last frost, in full sun. Travis is a rose-skinned sweet potato noted in university cultivar trial descriptions as both an orange-fleshed early type and, in white-fleshed seed strains, a high-yielding market and garden variety distributed through North Carolina Foundation Seed Producers; either way it is valued for its earlier maturity relative to standard-season types like Beauregard. The vines are productive and the roots size up quickly enough to allow an earlier first harvest window in short-season gardens. Dig as soon as roots reach usable size to beat frost, then cure in warm, humid conditions for roughly a week before moving to cool storage.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

common_name: Pelican Processor Sweet Potato (Louisiana Canning Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost; Pelican Processor was bred in Louisiana for the canning and processing industry, with cream skin and light cream flesh that holds its color and shape after cooking.

directions: Set rooted slips into ridged, well-drained soil two to four weeks after the last frost. Pelican Processor was developed by Louisiana sweet potato breeders specifically for the canning and processing trade, producing cream-skinned roots with light cream flesh that stays firm and holds its shape well after cooking rather than breaking down into the soft, custardy texture typical of deep-orange baking types. Home gardeners who want sweet potatoes for frying, dicing, or canning rather than for traditional baked orange-flesh dishes may find it a useful change of pace from standard Beauregard-type roots. Harvest before frost, cure for about a week in warm, humid conditions, and store cool and dry.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

common_name: Georgia Red Sweet Potato (Coppery-Red Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost into loose, ridged soil; Georgia Red is an old Southern heirloom valued for its coppery-red skin and strong keeping quality.

directions: Plant slips into raised, loosened ridges two to four weeks after the last frost date, in full sun. Georgia Red is a traditional Southern dooryard heirloom, distinct from the red-skinned 'Georgia Jet' hybrid, grown for its coppery-red skin and reputation among older growers for holding up in storage longer than many softer-fleshed heirloom types. Vines are rangy and roots form somewhat irregularly, so hill soil generously through the season to keep developing roots covered. Dig before frost, cure about a week at warm, humid conditions to firm the skin and sweeten the flesh, then store in a cool, dry spot.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

common_name: Brazilian Crookneck Squash (Giant Curved-Neck Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Brazilian Crookneck is a giant, long-vined heirloom crookneck type that needs generous room and a full warm season to size up its 10-20 pound fruit.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once the soil has warmed well after the last frost, allowing the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Brazilian Crookneck is a South American heirloom crookneck squash producing some of the largest fruit in the moschata group, with pale tan to gray-tan skin, a long curving neck, and dense, deep orange flesh with a nutty, sweet flavor well suited to roasting or soup. Like other moschata squashes it carries better resistance to squash vine borer and bacterial wilt than most pepo types, making it a dependable choice where those pests are a problem. Let fruit mature fully on the vine until the rind resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Loche is a Peruvian landrace squash grown almost exclusively around Lambayeque, prized for its dense, starchy, nutty-flavored flesh used fresh rather than cured and stored.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills after danger of frost has passed, in warm, fertile soil. Loche is a distinctive elongated, dumbbell-shaped squash landrace long grown around Lambayeque in northern Peru, where it is a signature ingredient in regional dishes such as arroz con pato and causa rather than a storage squash; its dense, pale, nutty-flavored flesh is normally cooked fresh rather than cured for long keeping. The crop has a reputation for growing true to type only in its home region, with fruit grown elsewhere from the same seed often reverting toward more typical moschata shapes. Harvest once the skin has toughened and the characteristic curved, narrow-waisted shape has filled out, and use the flesh promptly for best flavor and texture.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
International Potato Center (Peru) crop diversity records

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Betternut 900 is a later, higher-yielding hybrid update to the older Betternut 401 butternut, producing uniform 1.5-2 pound fruit.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills after the last frost, once soil has warmed thoroughly. Betternut 900 is a hybrid butternut bred as a successor to the older Betternut 401, holding the same compact, personal-sized 1.5-to-2-pound fruit but with improved yield, a smaller seed cavity, and tan skin over deep orange, dense flesh. Vines are semi-vigorous and set fruit uniformly, making this a reliable choice for gardeners who want small butternuts sized for single meals without the sprawl of full-size vines. Harvest once the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail, cure for one to two weeks, then move to cool, dry storage.
sources: NC State University Extension vegetable variety trials

common_name: Musquée de Maroc Squash (Moroccan Warted Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Musquée de Maroc is a Moroccan heirloom distinguished from the smoother Musquée de Provence by its heavily warted, deeply ribbed rind.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once soil has warmed well after the last frost, giving vines ample room to sprawl. Musquée de Maroc is a Moroccan heirloom winter squash related to the better-known Musquée de Provence but set apart by its rough, heavily warted, deeply ribbed, orange-red rind, which encloses dense, sweet, deep orange flesh prized for roasting and soup. Fruits run large, commonly 15 to 25 pounds, so give hills generous spacing and a full warm season to finish. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the stem has begun to dry, cure for a couple of weeks, then store in a cool, dry spot where it keeps for months.

common_name: Pennsylvania Dutch Crookneck Squash (Colonial Mid-Atlantic Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; this colonial-era Mid-Atlantic heirloom, also called Neck Pumpkin, produces a long curved neck with buff skin and deep orange flesh.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills after danger of frost has passed, once the soil has warmed thoroughly. Pennsylvania Dutch Crookneck, also known regionally as Neck Pumpkin, is one of the oldest named moschata squashes still grown in North America, dating to colonial-era Mid-Atlantic farms, with long curving necks, buff to tan skin, and deep orange flesh that bakes dry and sweet. Because the seed cavity sits low in the bulbous blossom end, most of the fruit is solid, usable neck, giving a high yield of flesh per squash. Allow fruit to fully harden on the vine before cutting with a few inches of stem attached, cure in a warm spot for one to two weeks, then store in a cool, dry location where it keeps well into winter.

common_name: Calabaza de Castilla Squash (Mexican Mottled Calabaza)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Calabaza de Castilla is a Mexican and Central American calabaza-type heirloom with mottled green-and-cream rind, traditionally cooked into candied calabaza en tacha.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once soil has warmed thoroughly after the last frost. Calabaza de Castilla is a traditional Mexican and Central American calabaza heirloom, flattened and ribbed in form with a mottled green-and-cream rind that often turns more tan as it cures, enclosing sweet, fine-grained orange flesh. It is the type most associated with calabaza en tacha, the whole or sliced squash slow-candied in piloncillo syrup for Day of the Dead celebrations, though it is equally good roasted or added to soups. Harvest once the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail, cure for a week or two in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location for long keeping.
